explanation: UCC § 2-315 creates the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose when the seller has reason to know both the buyer's particular purpose for the goods and that the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment to select suitable goods. Merchant status is not required, so the options adding a merchant requirement are incorrect, and option A omits the seller's knowledge requirement.

quotes.quote: Where the seller at the time of contracting has reason to know any particular purpose for which the goods are required and that the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment to select or furnish suitable goods, there is unless excluded or modified under the next section an implied warranty that the goods shall be fit for such purpose.

explanation: Under IRC § 469(i), Smith's $25,000 special allowance for rental real estate is reduced by 50% of AGI over $100,000. Because Smith's AGI (determined without regard to the passive loss) is $120,000, the allowance is reduced by $10,000 to $15,000, so only $15,000 of the $40,000 rental loss is currently deductible; the rest is carried forward.

quotes.quote: In the case of any natural person, subsection (a) shall not apply to that portion of the passive activity loss or the deduction equivalent (within the meaning of subsection (j)(5)) of the passive activity credit for any taxable year which is attributable to all rental real estate activities with respect to which such individual actively participated in such taxable year (and if any portion of such loss or credit arose in another taxable year, in such other taxable year).

The aggregate amount to which paragraph (1) applies for any taxable year shall not exceed $25,000. (3) Phase-out of exemption (A) In general In the case of any taxpayer, the $25,000 amount under paragraph (2) shall be reduced (but not below zero) by 50 percent of the amount by which the adjusted gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year exceeds $100,000.

adjusted gross income shall be determined without regard to— (i) any amount includible in gross income under section 86, (ii) the amounts excludable from gross income under sections 85(c), 135, and 137, (iii) the amounts allowable as a deduction under sections 219, 221, and 250, and (iv) any passive activity loss or any loss allowable by reason of subsection (c)(7).

explanation: An S corporation shareholder reports their pro rata share of the corporation's taxable income whether or not it is distributed. Carson's 40% share of the $400,000 taxable income is $160,000. The $28,000 cash distribution (40% of $70,000) would generally not add income for an S corporation shareholder, so the reported amount is $160,000, not $188,000.

quotes.quote: In determining the tax under this chapter of a shareholder for the shareholder’s taxable year in which the taxable year of the S corporation ends ... there shall be taken into account the shareholder’s pro rata share of the corporation’s— (A) items of income (including tax-exempt income), loss, deduction, or credit the separate treatment of which could affect the liability for tax of any shareholder, and (B) nonseparately computed income or loss.

An S corporation must report, and a shareholder is required to take into account in the shareholder's return, the shareholder's pro rata share, whether or not distributed, of the S corporation's items of income, loss, deduction, or credit described in paragraphs (a)(2), (3), and (4) of this section.

explanation: Under section 704(c), the built-in gain at contribution ($40,000, the excess of the land's $100,000 FMV over Acre's $60,000 basis) must be allocated to Acre. The remaining $60,000 of appreciation occurring after contribution is allocated under the partnership agreement, so it is shared equally by all partners, giving Acre $40,000 + $20,000 and the other partners $20,000 each.

quotes.quote: income, gain, loss, and deduction with respect to property contributed to the partnership by a partner shall be shared among the partners so as to take account of the variation between the basis of the property to the partnership and its fair market value at the time of contribution
Under this rule , if the partnership sells section 704(c) property and recognizes gain or loss , built-in gain or loss on the property is allocated to the contributing partner .

Under paragraph (b)(1) of this section, only $5,400 of gain must be allocated to A to account for A's built-in gain . The remaining $1,000 of gain is allocated equally between A and B in accordance with the partnership agreement .

explanation: FUTA imposes an excise tax only on employers, not employees, and the actual unemployment insurance system is a federal-state program in which states administer their own unemployment compensation laws. State laws are submitted to and approved by the Secretary of Labor under IRC § 3304, confirming that the system is administered by the states through their employment laws.

quotes.quote: There is hereby imposed on every employer (as defined in section 3306(a)) for each calendar year an excise tax, with respect to having individuals in his employ, equal to 6 percent of the total wages (as defined in section 3306(b)) paid by such employer during the calendar year with respect to employment (as defined in section 3306(c)).
States may at their option submit their unemployment compensation laws for approval (section 3304(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 ).

explanation: Decker's realized gain is $500,000 amount realized minus $200,000 cost basis, or $300,000. Under IRC § 121(a), gain from the sale of a principal residence owned and used for at least two of the prior five years is excluded from gross income, but for a single taxpayer the exclusion is limited to $250,000 under § 121(b)(1), leaving $50,000 of gain to recognize. The purchase of a new house does not defer the gain; the old rollover provision was repealed.

quotes.quote: The gain from the sale or other disposition of property shall be the excess of the amount realized therefrom over the adjusted basis provided in section 1011 for determining gain
The amount of gain excluded from gross income under subsection (a) with respect to any sale or exchange shall not exceed $250,000.

explanation: A partnership terminates only if no part of its business continues to be carried on by any partner in a partnership; here the business continued with Ross and Taylor. Even under the pre-2018 50% sale-or-exchange rule, Stone sold only a 35% interest, which is below the 50% threshold, so no termination occurred on April 9 or any other date.

quotes.quote: a partnership shall be considered as terminated only if no part of any business, financial operation, or venture of the partnership continues to be carried on by any of its partners in a partnership.

A partnership shall terminate when 50 percent or more of the total interest in partnership capital and profits is sold or exchanged within a period of 12 consecutive months. Such sale or exchange includes a sale or exchange to another member of the partnership.

explanation: The municipal bond interest is excludable from gross income under IRC §103, so it must be subtracted in the Schedule M-1 reconciliation. The year 1 state franchise tax refund is a recovery of a previously deducted tax and is excluded under IRC §111 only to the extent the prior deduction did not reduce tax; because it was deducted and produced a tax benefit, it stays in taxable income, so no M-1 adjustment is made for it. Thus taxable income is $500,000 − $7,500 = $492,500.

quotes.quote: Except as provided in subsection (b), gross income does not include interest on any State or local bond

Gross income does not include income attributable to the recovery during the taxable year of any amount deducted in any prior taxable year to the extent such amount did not reduce the amount of tax imposed by this chapter.

Recoveries result from the receipt of amounts in respect of the previously deducted or credited section 111 items, such as from the collection or sale of a bad debt, refund or credit of taxes paid, or cancellation of taxes accrued.

explanation: Because this was a liquidating distribution, Gulde's basis in the land is determined under IRC 732(b): the partner's outside basis ($26,000) reduced by the cash distributed ($12,000), or $14,000. Under 732(c), that $14,000 is allocated to the only noncash property, the land, so its basis becomes $14,000 rather than Chyme's $10,000 inside basis.

quotes.quote: The basis of property (other than money ) distributed by a partnership to a partner in liquidation of the partner’s interest shall be an amount equal to the adjusted basis of such partner’s interest in the partnership reduced by any money distributed in the same transaction.

to the extent of any basis remaining after the allocation under subparagraph (A), to other distributed properties— (i) first by assigning to each such other property such other property’s adjusted basis to the partnership, and (ii) then, to the extent any increase or decrease in basis is required in order to have the adjusted bases of such other distributed properties equal such remaining basis, in the manner provided in paragraph (2) or (3), whichever is appropriate.

explanation: IRC §57(a) lists the items of tax preference for AMT purposes. Percentage depletion in excess of the property's adjusted basis is a tax preference item, while long-term capital gain and ordinary dividends are not listed as items of tax preference for individuals, so only the $9,000 depletion excess counts.

quotes.quote: With respect to each property (as defined in section 614), the excess of the deduction for depletion allowable under section 611 for the taxable year over the adjusted basis of the property at the end of the taxable year (determined without regard to the depletion deduction for the taxable year).
For purposes of this part, the items of tax preference determined under this section are— (1) Depletion

explanation: Under §25.2511-1(h)(8), a gift occurs when the insured pays premiums on a policy payable to others only if the insured retains no power to change the beneficiaries or revest the economic benefits in himself. Because the taxpayer owns the contract on his own life, he retains control over the beneficiary designation, so no completed gift has been made for gift tax purposes.

quotes.quote: If the insured purchases a life insurance policy, or pays a premium on a previously issued policy, the proceeds of which are payable to a beneficiary or beneficiaries other than his estate, and with respect to which the insured retains no reversionary interest in himself or his estate and no power to revest the economic benefits in himself or his estate or to change the beneficiaries or their proportionate benefits ... the insured has made a gift of the value of the policy, or to the extent of the premium paid

explanation: For a position with respect to a tax shelter or reportable transaction, the section 6694(a) preparer penalty applies unless it is reasonable to believe the position would more likely than not be sustained on its merits. Disclosure alone does not lower the standard to substantial authority or reasonable basis for tax shelters.

quotes.quote: If the position is with respect to a tax shelter (as defined in section 6662(d)(2)(C)(ii) ) or a reportable transaction to which section 6662A applies, the position is described in this paragraph unless it is reasonable to believe that the position would more likely than not be sustained on its merits.

The position is with respect to a tax shelter (as defined in section 6662(d)(2)(C)(ii)) or a reportable transaction to which section 6662A applies, and it was not reasonable to believe that the position would more likely than not be sustained on its merits;

explanation: Under IRC § 6075(a), the federal estate tax return must be filed within 9 months after the decedent's death. Treasury Regulation § 20.6075-1 makes the due date the day in the ninth calendar month numerically corresponding to the date of death, so a May 15 death produces a February 15 due date (here, February 15, year 3).

quotes.quote: Returns made under section 6018(a) (relating to estate taxes) shall be filed within 9 months after the date of the decedent’s death.

The due date, for a decedent dying after December 31, 1970, is, unless an extension of time for filing has been obtained, the day of the ninth calendar month after the decedent's death numerically corresponding to the day of the calendar month on which death occurred.

explanation: Under IRC § 704(a), a partner's distributive share is determined by the partnership agreement, and Aston and Becker are equal partners, so Aston's share of the $20,000 of ordinary income is 50% = $10,000. The $12,000 long-term capital gain is separately stated under § 702(a)(2), and the $5,000 distribution affects basis rather than Aston's share of ordinary income.

quotes.quote: A partner’s distributive share of income, gain, loss, deduction, or credit shall, except as otherwise provided in this chapter, be determined by the partnership agreement.

each partner shall take into account separately his distributive share of the partnership’s— (1) gains and losses from sales or exchanges of capital assets held for not more than 1 year, (2) gains and losses from sales or exchanges of capital assets held for more than 1 year

explanation: Under IRC §6511(a), when no return was filed, a claim for credit or refund must be filed within 2 years from the time the tax was paid. Since the individual did not file a return, the normal 3-year-from-filing period never started, and the 2-year-from-payment limit applies.

quotes.quote: Claim for credit or refund of an overpayment of any tax imposed by this title in respect of which tax the taxpayer is required to file a return shall be filed by the taxpayer within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever of such periods expires the later, or if no return was filed by the taxpayer, within 2 years from the time the tax was paid.
(2) If no return is filed, the claim for credit or refund of an overpayment must be filed by the taxpayer within 2 years from the time the tax was paid.

explanation: Vale must include her 50% distributive share of Ball's dividend income, $6,000, in gross income. The $40,000 share of tax-exempt interest keeps its exempt character under § 702(b) and is excluded from gross income, while the $10,000 cash distribution produces no gain under § 731(a)(1) because it does not exceed Vale's basis (her $60,000 beginning basis plus her share of current-year income).

quotes.quote: The character of any item of income, gain, loss, deduction, or credit included in a partner’s distributive share under paragraphs (1) through (7) of subsection (a) shall be determined as if such item were realized directly from the source from which realized by the partnership, or incurred in the same manner as incurred by the partnership.
Except as provided in subsection (b), gross income does not include interest on any State or local bond.

explanation: IRC § 6695 expressly imposes assessable penalties on tax return preparers for failing to furnish a copy to the taxpayer, failing to sign the return, and failing to retain a copy or list under § 6107, but neither the Code nor the regulations impose a penalty for failing to notify a taxpayer about an inadvertent error on a return filed 10 years ago.

quotes.quote: (a) Failure to furnish copy to taxpayer Any person who is a tax return preparer with respect to any return or claim for refund who fails to comply with section 6107(a) with respect to such return or claim shall pay a penalty of $50 for such failure

(b) Failure to sign return Any person who is a tax return preparer with respect to any return or claim for refund , who is required by regulations prescribed by the Secretary to sign such return or claim, and who fails to comply with such regulations with respect to such return or claim shall pay a penalty of $50 for such failure

(d) Failure to retain copy or list Any person who is a tax return preparer with respect to any return or claim for refund who fails to comply with section 6107(b) with respect to such return or claim shall pay a penalty of $50 for each such failure

explanation: Under IRC §357(c), when a taxpayer transfers property to a controlled corporation in a §351 exchange, any excess of the assumed (or subject-to) liabilities over the adjusted basis of the transferred property is recognized as gain. Here the $12,000 liability exceeds the $6,000 basis by $6,000, so the shareholder recognizes $6,000 of gain.

quotes.quote: if the sum of the amount of the liabilities assumed exceeds the total of the adjusted basis of the property transferred pursuant to such exchange, then such excess shall be considered as a gain from the sale or exchange of a capital asset or of property which is not a capital asset, as the case may be.

if the sum of the amount of liabilities assumed plus the amount of liabilities to which the property is subject exceeds the total of the adjusted basis of the property transferred pursuant to such exchange, then such excess shall be considered as a gain from the sale or exchange of a capital asset or of property which is not a capital asset as the case may be.

explanation: Jackson, a merchant, made a signed written offer that gave assurance it would be held open, so UCC § 2-205 made the offer irrevocable for a reasonable time despite the lack of an expiration date; the day 4 revocation was therefore ineffective. Because the offer invited acceptance by any reasonable medium and was itself mailed, Sands' mailed acceptance on day 7 was reasonable, and under the mailbox rule it became effective when mailed, even though Jackson received it later.

quotes.quote: An offer by a merchant to buy or sell goods in a signed writing which by its terms gives assurance that it will be held open is not revocable, for lack of consideration, during the time stated or if no time is stated for a reasonable time, but in no event may such period of irrevocability exceed three months
an offer to make a contract shall be construed as inviting acceptance in any manner and by any medium reasonable in the circumstances
Under the mailbox rule, an offer is considered accepted the moment the offeree mails their letter, rather than when the offeror receives the letter in the mail.

explanation: Section 248 allows corporations to amortize organizational expenditures, and Treasury Regulation §1.248-1(b)(2) expressly lists incorporation services, temporary directors' fees, and organizational meeting costs as amortizable examples. The same regulation expressly excludes stock issuance costs from the definition of organizational expenditures, so they cannot be amortized under section 248.

quotes.quote: expenses of temporary directors and of organizational meetings of directors or stockholders; and fees paid to the State of incorporation.

Expenditures connected with issuing or selling shares of stock or other securities , such as commissions , professional fees, and printing costs . This is so even where the particular issue of stock to which the expenditures relate is for a fixed term of years ;

explanation: Long's authority as Frost's agent terminated by operation of law when Frost was judicially declared incompetent, so Long could no longer bind Frost; the fact that both Long and Grant were unaware of the incompetence does not revive that authority. Since no durable power or authority coupled with an interest appears, Frost or Frost's legal representative would not be liable.

quotes.source: Cornell LII Wex, power of attorney
quotes.quote: Typically, a power of attorney only remains effective as long as the principal is alive and competent to make decisions. Principals may, however, grant durable powers of attorney that persist after they are no longer able to make their own decisions.

Unless displaced by the particular provisions of the Uniform Commercial Code , the principles of law and equity, including the law merchant and the law relative to capacity to contract , principal and agent, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, and other validating or invalidating cause supplement its provisions.

explanation: Under § 1015(a), the child takes the donor's $40,000 basis for computing gain but a $30,000 fair-market-value basis for computing loss. Because the $36,000 sale price falls between those two figures, no gain or loss is recognized.

quotes.quote: If the property was acquired by gift after December 31, 1920 , the basis shall be the same as it would be in the hands of the donor or the last preceding owner by whom it was not acquired by gift, except that if such basis (adjusted for the period before the date of the gift as provided in section 1016) is greater than the fair market value of the property at the time of the gift, then for the purpose of determining loss the basis shall be such fair market value.

A acquires by gift income-producing property which has an adjusted basis of $100,000 at the date of gift. The fair market value of the property at the date of gift is $90,000. A later sells the property for $95,000. In such case there is neither gain nor loss . The basis for determining loss is $90,000; therefore, there is no loss . Furthermore, there is no gain , since the basis for determining gain is $100,000.

explanation: Lemon's original basis was $21,000 (2,000 shares x $10.50). The 5% stock dividend (100 shares) was nontaxable under §305(a), so under §307(a) the $21,000 basis is allocated over 2,100 shares, giving $10 per share. The 2-for-1 split doubled the shares to 4,200 while leaving total basis at $21,000, giving $5 per share; therefore 800 shares sold have a basis of $4,000 (800 x $5).

quotes.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, gross income does not include the amount of any distribution of the stock of a corporation made by such corporation to its shareholders with respect to its stock.

If a shareholder in a corporation receives its stock or rights to acquire its stock (referred to in this subsection as “new stock”) in a distribution to which section 305(a) applies, then the basis of such new stock and of the stock with respect to which it is distributed (referred to in this section as “old stock”), respectively, shall, in the shareholder’s hands, be determined by allocating between the old stock and the new stock the adjusted basis of the old stock.

If a shareholder receives stock or stock rights as a distribution on stock previously held and under section 305 such distribution is not includible in gross income then, except as provided in section 307(b) and § 1.307-2 , the basis of the stock with respect to which the distribution was made shall be allocated between the old and new stocks or rights in proportion to the fair market values of each on the date of distribution.

explanation: A preparer generally may rely on client-furnished information, but Treasury Regulations require the preparer to make appropriate inquiries when a Code section conditions a deduction on specific facts or documentation. Business travel expenses must be substantiated under IRC § 274(d), so the CPA’s failure to inquire about documentation can expose the CPA to a tax return preparer penalty under § 6694; it does not, by itself, establish a fraudulent return or relieve the client of penalties.

quotes.quote: The tax return preparer must make reasonable inquiries if the information as furnished appears to be incorrect or incomplete. Additionally, some provisions of the Code or regulations require that specific facts and circumstances exist (for example , that the taxpayer maintain specific documents) before a deduction or credit may be claimed. The tax return preparer must make appropriate inquiries to determine the existence of facts and circumstances required by a Code section or regulation as a condition of the claiming of a deduction or credit .

No deduction or credit shall be allowed— (1) under section 162 or 212 for any traveling expense (including meals and lodging while away from home), (2) for any expense for gifts , or (3) with respect to any listed property (as defined in section 280F(d)(4) ), unless the taxpayer substantiates by adequate records or by sufficient evidence corroborating the taxpayer’s own statement

explanation: Under IRC § 472(b)(1), LIFO treats ending inventory as consisting of the oldest goods (those in opening inventory in order of acquisition) before current-year acquisitions. Option A reverses LIFO's effect in rising prices, Option B is wrong because § 472(e) requires continued use without annual IRS permission once elected, and Option C is wrong because § 472(c) generally requires LIFO conformity for shareholder reports and credit statements.

quotes.quote: (1) Treat those remaining on hand at the close of the taxable year as being: First, those included in the opening inventory of the taxable year (in the order of acquisition) to the extent thereof; and second, those acquired in the taxable year;

explanation: The general limitations period for assessment is three years after the return is filed, and the agent found no fraud or substantial omission that would extend that period. By year 6, the earliest years in the proposed adjustment are outside that three-year window, so the adjustment is improper for those closed years; disallowance of personal jet use is also not a change in accounting method that would avoid the limitations period.

quotes.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, the amount of any tax imposed by this title shall be assessed within 3 years after the return was filed (whether or not such return was filed on or after the date prescribed)...
The amount of any tax imposed by the Code (other than a tax collected by means of stamps) shall be assessed within 3 years after the return was filed.

explanation: Impossibility (or impracticability) of performance discharges a party's contractual duty by operation of law when an unforeseen event after contracting makes performance impossible, as reflected in UCC 2-615's excuse for impracticability. Novation and accord and satisfaction discharge duties by agreement, and anticipatory repudiation is a breach giving remedies rather than a discharge by operation of law.

quotes.quote: Delay in delivery or non-delivery in whole or in part by a seller who complies with paragraphs (b) and (c) is not a breach of his duty under a contract for sale if performance as agreed has been made impracticable by the occurrence of a contingency the non-occurrence of which was a basic assumption on which the contract was made or by compliance in good faith with any applicable foreign or domestic governmental regulation or order whether or not it later proves to be invalid.
Under contract law, a party can raise an impossibility defense when an unforeseen event occurs after the contract is made which makes performance impossible.

explanation: Under § 1015(a) and the regulations, when the donor's adjusted basis ($10,000) exceeds the property's fair market value at the time of the gift ($9,000), the donee's basis for determining loss is that lower fair market value. Because the child sold for $7,000, the transaction is a loss sale, so the basis used is $9,000, producing a $2,000 loss.

quotes.quote: except that if such basis (adjusted for the period before the date of the gift as provided in section 1016) is greater than the fair market value of the property at the time of the gift, then for the purpose of determining loss the basis shall be such fair market value.

The same rule applies in determining loss unless the basis (adjusted for the period prior to the date of gift in accordance with sections 1016 and 1017) is greater than the fair market value of the property at the time of the gift. In such case, the basis for determining loss is the fair market value at the time of the gift.

explanation: Municipal bond interest is tax-exempt income that increases S corporation stock basis under § 1367(a)(1)(A). Applying the ordering rules in Reg. § 1.1367-1(f), basis is increased by the $2,000 tax-exempt income first, then reduced by the $6,000 distribution, and finally reduced by the $5,000 ordinary loss: $15,000 + $2,000 - $6,000 - $5,000 = $6,000.

quotes.quote: For any taxable year of a corporation beginning on or after August 18, 1998, except as provided in paragraph (g) of this section, the adjustments required by section 1367(a) are made in the following order— (1) Any increase in basis attributable to the income items described in section 1367(a)(1)(A) and (B), and the excess of the deductions for depletion described in section 1367(a)(1)(C); (2) Any decrease in basis attributable to a distribution by the corporation described in section 1367(a)(2)(A); (3) Any decrease in basis attributable to noncapital, nondeductible expenses described in section 1367(a)(2)(D), and the oil and gas depletion deduction described in section 1367(a)(2)(E); and (4) Any decrease in basis attributable to items of loss or deduction described in section 1367(a)(2)(B) and (C).

explanation: Section 1221 defines a capital asset as all property held by a taxpayer except for specific exclusions, including inventory, depreciable business property such as machinery and equipment, and accounts receivable acquired in the ordinary course of business. Marketable securities held by an individual business owner are not among those exclusions and therefore are generally capital assets.

quotes.quote: the term “ capital asset ” means property held by the taxpayer (whether or not connected with his trade or business), but does not include— (1) stock in trade of the taxpayer or other property of a kind which would properly be included in the inventory of the taxpayer if on hand at the close of the taxable year, or property held by the taxpayer primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of his trade or business; (2) property, used in his trade or business, of a character which is subject to the allowance for depreciation provided in section 167, or real property used in his trade or business; ... (4) accounts or notes receivable acquired in the ordinary course of trade or business for services rendered or from the sale of property described in paragraph (1)
The term capital assets includes all classes of property not specifically excluded by section 1221.

explanation: Section 1244's $50,000 annual ordinary-loss limit applies to losses sustained in the current year; the prior-year NOL carryover (even though it included a Sec. 1244 loss) is separately deductible and does not reduce the current year's Sec. 1244 ordinary loss. The regulation's example with nearly identical facts expressly allows the full $50,000 current Sec. 1244 loss as ordinary plus the full NOL carryover.

quotes.quote: A taxpayer may deduct the maximum of ordinary loss permitted under section 1244(b) even though all or a portion of the taxpayer 's net operating loss carryback or carryover for the taxable year was, when incurred, a loss on section 1244 stock .
A may deduct the full $50,000 as an ordinary loss under section 1244 and the full $15,000 as a net operating loss carryover in 1981.

explanation: Treasury Circular 230, 31 CFR § 10.21, requires a practitioner who knows a client made an error in a return already submitted to advise the client promptly of the error and its consequences; it does not impose a 30-day amended-return deadline, require only workpaper documentation, or require resignation.

quotes.quote: A practitioner who, having been retained by a client with respect to a matter administered by the Internal Revenue Service , knows that the client has not complied with the revenue laws of the United States or has made an error in or omission from any return, document, affidavit, or other paper which the client submitted or executed under the revenue laws of the United States, must advise the client promptly of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission. The practitioner must advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission.

explanation: DNI is the trust's taxable income before the distribution deduction and personal exemption, then modified to exclude capital gains allocated to corpus and not distributed. Taxable income before that modification is $2,500 + $2,000 + $5,000 − $500 − $750 = $8,250; excluding the $5,000 corpus capital gain leaves $3,250.

quotes.quote: Gains from the sale or exchange of capital assets shall be excluded to the extent that such gains are allocated to corpus and are not (A) paid, credited, or required to be distributed to any beneficiary during the taxable year, or (B) paid, permanently set aside, or to be used for the purposes specified in section 642(c).

Except as provided in § 1.643(a)-6 and paragraph (b) of this section, gains from the sale or exchange of capital assets are ordinarily excluded from distributable net income and are not ordinarily considered as paid , credited, or required to be distributed to any beneficiary.

explanation: Treasury Regulation § 301.7701-15(f)(1)(x) expressly excludes from the definition of tax return preparer an individual preparing a return for a trust or estate of which the individual is a fiduciary. Joe, as trustee, is a fiduciary of the trust, so he is not considered a tax return preparer when preparing Form 1041, regardless of compensation or beneficiary permission.

quotes.quote: An individual preparing a return or claim for refund for a trust, estate, or other entity of which the individual either is a fiduciary or is an officer, general partner, or employee of the fiduciary .

explanation: In a like-kind exchange, the taxpayer's basis in the replacement property equals the basis of the relinquished property, increased by liabilities assumed and decreased by liabilities relieved (treated as money received), plus any gain recognized. Vinton's basis is $300,000 + $230,000 (apartment building mortgage assumed) - $100,000 (land mortgage assumed by the other party) + $0 gain recognized = $430,000. The realized gain of $120,000 is not recognized because Vinton assumed more debt ($230,000) than he was relieved of ($100,000), so he received no net boot.

quotes.quote: the basis shall be the same as that of the property exchanged, decreased in the amount of any money received by the taxpayer and increased in the amount of gain or decreased in the amount of loss to the taxpayer that was recognized on such exchange.

explanation: Rigg can be the common parent because it directly owns 85% of Steele, satisfying the 80% voting-and-value test. Urco qualifies because the stock-meeting-80% requirement is met by direct ownership of Urco by one or more of the other includible corporations: Rigg's 40% plus Steele's 50% equals 90% direct ownership. All three are includible C corporations, so Rigg, Steele, and Urco are an affiliated group eligible to file consolidated returns.

quotes.quote: (A) 1 or more chains of includible corporations connected through stock ownership with a common parent corporation which is an includible corporation , but only if— (B) (i) the common parent owns directly stock meeting the requirements of paragraph (2) in at least 1 of the other includible corporations , and (ii) stock meeting the requirements of paragraph (2) in each of the includible corporations (except the common parent) is owned directly by 1 or more of the other includible corporations . (2) 80-percent voting and value test The ownership of stock of any corporation meets the requirements of this paragraph if it— (A) possesses at least 80 percent of the total voting power of the stock of such corporation, and (B) has a value equal to at least 80 percent of the total value of the stock of such corporation.

explanation: Prime starts with book income of $300,000. The corporate bond interest is taxable and already included in book income, so no M-1 adjustment is needed for it. The $20,000 term life insurance premium is disallowed under IRC § 264(a)(1) because Prime is the policy owner and beneficiary, so it is added back, producing taxable income of $320,000.

quotes.quote: No deduction shall be allowed for— (1) Premiums on any life insurance policy, or endowment or annuity contract, if the taxpayer is directly or indirectly a beneficiary under the policy or contract.

Premiums paid by a taxpayer on a life insurance policy are not deductible from the taxpayer 's gross income , even though they would otherwise be deductible as trade or business expenses , if they are paid on a life insurance policy covering the life of any officer or employee of the taxpayer , or any person (including the taxpayer ) who is financially interested in any trade or business carried on by the taxpayer , when the taxpayer is directly or indirectly a beneficiary of the policy.

explanation: A general partner ordinarily has the right to participate in management, to inspect partnership books and records, and, as an agent of the partnership, to contract on its behalf within the scope of the partnership business. A general partner is not entitled to be liable only for personal negligence; general partners are personally liable for the obligations of the partnership generally, not merely for their own negligent acts.

quotes.quote: Partnerships are composed of partners , who are agents of the partnership and may enter into contracts on behalf of the partnership.

explanation: Strom's initial basis is his $16,000 adjusted basis in the land, reduced by the portion of the $24,000 mortgage treated as assumed by the other partners (75% × $24,000 = $18,000). The resulting negative balance cannot reduce basis below zero, so the $2,000 excess is treated as capital gain under section 731(a), leaving Strom with a zero basis in Ace.

quotes.quote: If the contributed property is subject to indebtedness or if liabilities of the partner are assumed by the partnership, the basis of the contributing partner's interest shall be reduced by the portion of the indebtedness assumed by the other partners, since the partnership's assumption of his indebtedness is treated as a distribution of money to the partner.

If, in example 1 of this section, the property contributed by A was subject to a mortgage of $6,000, the basis of A's interest would be zero, computed as follows: Adjusted basis to A of property contributed $4,000 Less portion of mortgage assumed by other partners which must be treated as a distribution (80 percent of $6,000) 4,800 (800) Since A's basis cannot be less than zero, the $800 in excess of basis, which is considered as a distribution of money under section 752(b), is treated as capital gain from the sale or exchange or a partnership interest. See section 731(a).

explanation: Under §722 Skinner begins with $17,000 ($5,000 cash + $12,000 adjusted basis of the land). The partnership's assumption of the $10,000 mortgage is a deemed distribution of money under §752(b), but only to the extent assumed by the other partners: 80% x $10,000 = $8,000, reducing basis to $9,000. Skinner's 20% share of the partnership's $20,000 recourse liabilities is a deemed contribution of $4,000 under §752(a), so his final basis is $13,000.

quotes.quote: The basis of an interest in a partnership acquired by a contribution of property, including money, to the partnership shall be the amount of such money and the adjusted basis of such property to the contributing partner at the time of the contribution increased by the amount (if any) of gain recognized under section 721(b) to the contributing partner at such time.

(a) Increase in partner’s liabilities Any increase in a partner’s share of the liabilities of a partnership, or any increase in a partner’s individual liabilities by reason of the assumption by such partner of partnership liabilities, shall be considered as a contribution of money by such partner to the partnership. (b) Decrease in partner’s liabilities Any decrease in a partner’s share of the liabilities of a partnership, or any decrease in a partner’s individual liabilities by reason of the assumption by the partnership of such individual liabilities, shall be considered as a distribution of money to the partner by the partnership.

If the contributed property is subject to indebtedness or if liabilities of the partner are assumed by the partnership , the basis of the contributing partner 's interest shall be reduced by the portion of the indebtedness assumed by the other partners , since the partnership 's assumption of his indebtedness is treated as a distribution of money to the partner .
